front: Explain the difference between a rule-based system and a machine learning system, using a loan example.
back: A rule-based system applies rules a person wrote; a learning system finds the pattern from past files and their outcomes.

front: Name the two phases of a model's life and say which one is expensive.
back: Training and inference; training is the expensive one.

front: Is deep learning a way to learn, like supervised learning? Explain.
back: No. It is a type of model that can be trained in any of the three ways.

front: Give one task in a bank where you would write a rule instead of training a model.
back: For example checking that an applicant is of legal age.

front: Is "predict whether a customer repays" regression or classification? Why?
back: Classification: the answer is a category (repays or not).

front: Is "find groups of similar loan applicants" supervised or unsupervised?
back: Unsupervised: there is no right answer to learn from.

front: Give one loan example of anomaly detection.
back: Flagging an application whose pattern differs from all previous ones, as a fraud check.

front: What is the label in supervised learning?
back: The right answer y that comes with each training example.

front: In the offers table, what are m and n, and what is x^(3)?
What is the difference between a parameter and a hyperparameter? Give an example of each.
back: A parameter is learned (a weight w); a hyperparameter is chosen by you (the learning rate).

front: Why must a test set be used only once, at the end?
back: If you tune on it, it stops being unseen data and the score becomes too optimistic.

front: Give an example of leakage in a loan model.
back: Using "days in collections" to predict default: you only know it after the default has started.

front: For f(x) = 0.2 x + 30, what is the prediction at x = 100, and what does 30 mean?
back: 0.2 x 100 + 30 = 50; 30 is the prediction at x = 0, the bias.

front: Why do we square the errors instead of just adding them?
back: Plain errors above and below the line cancel each other, and squaring also punishes big misses.

front: Why can we not trust a fitted line far outside the data it saw?
back: The relationship may change outside that range, and the data has no evidence about it.

front: Compute J for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) and w = 2, b = 0.
back: The line predicts 2 and 4, the errors are 0, so J = 0.

front: Why divide by m? Why divide by 2?
back: Dividing by m makes the cost an average that does not depend on the amount of data; the 2 only cancels the 2 from the derivative.

front: What does convex mean, and why is it good news?
back: The cost has one bottom and no false valleys, so downhill always ends at the best solution.

front: A slope is positive. In which direction does w move, and why?
back: w moves left, to smaller values, because w := w - alpha x slope and the slope is positive.

front: You see the cost going up and down on successive iterations. Name two possible causes.
back: Alpha is too large (overshooting), or a bug such as a sign error.

front: Why does gradient descent slow down near the minimum even if alpha does not change?
back: The slope shrinks as you approach the bottom, so each step is smaller.

front: Do one step by hand for the points (1, 2), (2, 4) from w = 0, b = 0 with alpha = 0.1. What are w and b afterwards?
With n = 4 features, how many parameters does the model learn?
back: Five: four weights and the bias.

front: Give two reasons that np.dot beats a for loop.
back: Shorter code, and much faster because it uses compiled code and parallel hardware.

front: Why is the normal equation not enough for the rest of the course?
back: It only works for linear regression, while logistic regression and neural networks have no such formula.

front: Why does a feature measured in thousands make gradient descent slow?
back: The weight for that feature must be tiny, and the cost surface becomes a narrow valley that gradient descent zigzags across.

front: Z-score the value 1000 when the mean is 600 and the standard deviation is 450.
Why is polynomial regression still called linear regression?
back: Because it is linear in the weights, even though the features are powers of x.

front: Name two features you could build from the columns OfferedAmount and NumberOfTerms.
back: AmountPerTerm (amount divided by terms), and the logarithm of the amount.

front: Compute sigmoid(0) and say what it means.
back: 0.5: the model is undecided, and the input is on the decision boundary.

front: For w = [2, -1], b = 1 and x = [1, 3], what is z, and what does the model predict?
back: z = 2 x 1 - 1 x 3 + 1 = 0, so the probability is 0.5, exactly on the boundary.

front: Why can a straight line not be the model for yes or no data?
back: It gives values outside 0 and 1, and a single outlier can move its threshold.

front: A probability is 0.2. What are the odds?
Compute the loss for y = 1 when f = 0.8, and for y = 0 when f = 0.8.
Why is the cost exactly 0.693 at w = 0, b = 0?
back: Every prediction is 0.5, and -ln(0.5) = 0.693 for either label.

front: What changes between the gradient for linear and logistic regression?
back: Only the prediction f: a sigmoid in the logistic case.

front: Why does log loss punish a confident wrong answer so hard, and is that desirable?
back: The loss grows without limit as a wrong prediction approaches certainty. That is desirable, because it pushes the model to be calibrated: do not claim certainty you do not have.

front: Your training error is 2% and your validation error is 18%. What is the problem and what are two remedies?
back: High variance (overfitting). Remedies: more data, fewer features, a simpler model, more regularization.

front: What happens to the weights as lambda becomes very large?
back: They shrink towards zero and the model becomes almost flat (underfitting).

front: Why is a model that is perfect on its training data suspicious?
back: It may have memorized the noise, so it will probably do worse on new data.

front: In scikit-learn, which C corresponds to a lambda of 10?
A fraud model has 99% accuracy and the fraud rate is 1%. Is it good? What do you check?
back: Not necessarily: always predicting "no fraud" scores 99%. Check recall and precision for the fraud class, and compare with the baseline.

front: TP = 20, FP = 30, FN = 10. Compute precision and recall.
You lower the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3. What happens to precision and recall, and why?
back: Recall rises and precision usually falls, because more cases are flagged, including more wrong ones.

front: Why split loan data by date instead of randomly?
back: A random split lets the model train on data from after the cases it is tested on, which flatters it. Production only ever predicts the future.

front: Which algorithms in this chapter need feature scaling, and why?
back: KNN, SVM, neural networks, k-means and PCA, because they use distances or sums over features, so a feature measured in thousands would dominate.

front: Why does a random forest overfit less than one deep decision tree?
back: Many different trees vote, and their individual errors partly cancel (lower variance).

front: What is the difference between clustering and classification?
back: Classification has known labels and learns them; clustering has none and invents groups.

front: You have 3,000 loans and 20 columns. Which two models do you try first, and how do you pick?
back: A regularized logistic regression as the baseline and a random forest or gradient boosting, compared with cross-validation on a held-out set.

front: Why is logistic regression a one-neuron neural network?
back: A neuron is a weighted sum plus bias passed through an activation; with a sigmoid that is the logistic regression formula.

front: Why do hidden layers need a non-linear activation?
back: Otherwise stacked layers collapse into a single linear model and add no power.
The slope of the cost with respect to every weight, layer by layer, using the chain rule.

front: You have 5,000 rows of loan data. Do you start with a neural network? Why or why not?
back: No: with a small table, start with logistic regression and tree ensembles, which are simpler and usually as accurate; use neural networks for unstructured data or pretrained models.

front: A layer has 400 inputs and 25 neurons. How many parameters does it have?
back: 25 x (400 + 1) = 10,025: one weight per input plus one bias for each neuron.

front: X has 5 rows and 3 columns, and the layer has 4 neurons. What shape is X @ W + b?
back: 5 rows and 4 columns: one output per neuron for each example.

front: Compute the cosine similarity of [1, 0] and [0, 1], and of [2, 2] and [1, 1].
back: 0, and 1.

front: Derive the derivative of (w x - y) squared with respect to w.
back: 2 (w x - y) x, by the chain rule.

front: You run 40 tests at the 5% level on random data. About how many will look significant by chance?
A disease affects 1% of people. A test finds 90% of the sick and wrongly flags 9% of the healthy. If you test positive, what is the chance you are sick?
back: 0.9 x 0.01 = 0.009 of the sick flagged; 0.09 x 0.99 = 0.0891 of the healthy flagged; 0.009 / (0.009 + 0.0891) = about 9%. Most positives are false alarms because the disease is rare.

front: Name the three features that every definition of an agent shares.
back: An LLM, tools and some autonomy.

front: Which of the five patterns has no fixed end, and what does it therefore need?
back: The evaluator-optimizer, because it loops; it needs a stopping rule and a turn limit.

front: Give a loan example of routing.
back: Classify each message as a database question, a policy question or both, then send it down the matching path.

front: Why can an LLM not answer "what is 48,317 x 29" reliably on its own, and what fixes that?
back: LLMs generate text and can get arithmetic wrong; a code interpreter or calculator tool computes it exactly.

front: Which of Barry Zhang's four questions would stop you from building an agent for "approve or reject a loan automatically"?
back: The cost and discoverability of errors: a wrong approval is expensive and hard to notice, so keep a human in the loop and limit the agent's powers.

front: What are the three parts of an agent?
back: The environment, the tools and the system prompt.

front: Why should a safety rule be enforced in code and not in the prompt?
back: A prompt can be ignored or talked around; a read-only connection and a parser check cannot.

front: In the tool-use loop, what must a tool_result carry back, and where in the message does it go?
back: The tool_use_id of the call, the output as content, and is_error if it failed; the tool results come first in the new user message.

front: Why is hybrid search better than embeddings alone for a question about "Article 7"?
back: Embeddings are weak on exact strings; BM25 matches the literal term.

front: Compute the reciprocal rank fusion score of a chunk that is first in one list and third in another (k = 60).
What does contextual retrieval add to a chunk, and when?
back: A short LLM-written description of where the chunk sits in its document, prepended before embedding and before BM25 indexing.

front: Why measure hit@k before judging the generated answers?
back: If the right passage is not retrieved, no generator can answer correctly, so retrieval is measured on its own first.

Computes the slope of the cost for every weight in a network, layer by layer, with the chain rule
Running the inputs through the layers from left to right to get the prediction

A Python library for building neural networks in a few lines; it runs on TensorFlow, JAX or PyTorch
How mixed a group is: 1 minus the sum of squared class shares; a tree picks the split that lowers it most
Randomly switching off some neurons during training so the network cannot rely on any one
The network design behind LLMs: attention lets every word look at every other word
Letting a model generate more tokens while it thinks, which improves its answers
Everything the model can see at once: instructions, conversation, tool results; finite and priced per token
The name, description and parameters of a tool as the model sees them
The full sequence of messages and tool calls of one agent run; read it to debug
A workflow where a planner LLM decides the steps and hands them to workers
A writer LLM and a reviewer loop until a stopping rule is met; the pattern with the most agency
For text-to-SQL: whether the generated query returns the same rows as the gold query
Retrieval-augmented generation: look up passages first, then answer from them with citations
A passage of a document, the unit that is indexed and retrieved
A vector that represents the meaning of a text, so that similar texts are close together
How closely two vectors point the same way: 1 the same, 0 unrelated, -1 opposite

Merging ranked lists: each item earns 1 / (k + rank) from every list it appears in
